claims.text: The kitchen contains no gluten or animal products whatsoever, and the restaurant states it never brings wheat or animal-based ingredients into the shop, so cookware, utensils, and surfaces are used only for gluten-free cooking.
Because the kitchen handles no wheat at all, guests are asked to cooperate with a no-bring-in policy and not bring gluten or animal-based items into the dining area at table seating.
The Sanjo branch is described as fully vegan and fully gluten-free, presented as a venue designed specifically for guests with multiple dietary restrictions.
Unlike most Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, the soy-milk ramen broth here is made with gluten-free soy sauce.
Every menu item is 100% plant-based and the kitchen handles no animal products whatsoever, so there is no animal-ingredient cross-contact in the shop.
Reviewers describe the food as fully vegan, including sushi made with plant-based fish, with vegans fully catered for.
Beyond its gluten-free and vegan baseline, the restaurant says it can customize dishes for additional needs such as nut-free and mushroom-free when guests notify them in advance.
The owner is a pastry chef who built the business specifically around allergy-restricted diners, and notes that guests with allergies telling her they can eat safely is central to her mission.
The wheat-free, gluten-free design runs through the whole concept: original noodles are made from rice flour and kelp rather than wheat, and the broth uses gluten-free soy sauce.
A dedicated all-gluten-free, all-vegan kitchen with no wheat or animal products on site makes this a strong choice for celiac and vegan diners; reservations are recommended.
Reviewers call it one of the best vegan restaurants they have been to, with gyoza that have a delightful crunch and plant-based sushi that tastes delicious.

This is a fully dedicated gluten-free kitchen: it is described as an entirely wheat-free kitchen that does not use any gluten ingredients, with rice noodles used in place of wheat noodles. Because no wheat or gluten is handled anywhere in the kitchen, the usual ramen risk of shared boiling water, surfaces and utensils does not apply here.
Reviewers report that everything served is gluten-free and that they did not have to worry about cross-contamination, including in the soup.

As with any venue, practices can change and some residual cross-contamination risk can remain even at verified gluten-free restaurants — confirm directly with staff before ordering, especially if you are highly sensitive.

Because the entire kitchen is gluten-free and uses no wheat ingredients, the seasonings (including any soy sauce used) are gluten-free rather than standard wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce. This is consistent with the restaurant's 100% gluten-free designation, though the specific soy sauce brand is not documented; confirm with staff if you need certainty.
The restaurant is fully vegan — the broth is soy-milk based and dishes are entirely plant-based — so there is no animal product in the kitchen to cross-contact a vegan order.
Many dishes are also allium-free, which can help diners avoiding onion and garlic.
A reviewer noted the menu is very clearly labeled for all kinds of allergens, such as soy, gluten and wheat.

Suppliers are carefully selected and staff are described as trained in safe handling to protect guests with celiac disease or gluten intolerance; guests are also asked not to bring gluten-containing foods into the restaurant.
A rare find: a fully dedicated 100% gluten-free and vegan ramen restaurant, frequently described as one of the safest ramen options in Japan for people with celiac disease.
Fried items are made in this wheat-free kitchen, so the gyoza and okara croquettes are gluten-free — reviewers called the fried gyoza among the best they have had and the croquettes incredible.
The rice-flour gluten-free noodles drew praise for being cooked al dente and genuinely delicious rather than a compromise.
The shop also offers gluten-free, vegan cakes, reflecting the owner's background as an allergen-free pastry chef.

This is a fully dedicated gluten-free kitchen — no gluten ingredients are used anywhere on the premises, so the menu is built to be celiac-safe rather than relying on a few special items. As with any kitchen, confirm directly with staff if you have a severe reaction.
Everything here is made with rice flour, including the cakes, pastries and the rice bread used for sandwiches, so there is no wheat flour in the building.

The menu is dessert- and sweets-focused (cakes, dorayaki, matcha sweets, rice-bread sandwiches) rather than savory soy-sauce-based dishes, so wheat-containing soy sauce is unlikely to be a primary concern here. Still worth asking about any savory or seasoned item.

Vegan suitability is uncertain — the cafe's sweets and sandwiches commonly include dairy and egg (for example a ham-and-egg rice-bread sando), and no source confirms dedicated vegan preparation. Vegan diners should confirm specific items with staff.
Staff are described by visitors as welcoming and accommodating, and the cafe is run as a dedicated gluten-free space, which suggests genuine familiarity with celiac needs.
Carries a dedicated-facility / celiac-safe designation: 100% gluten-free with no gluten ingredients used on site.

Everything on the menu is gluten-free and made with rice flour, so the whole menu is open to celiac diners rather than just a handful of items — popular picks include the dorayaki, matcha sweets, cakes and rice-bread sandwiches.

name: Gion Soy Milk Ramen – Uno Yukiko

claims.text: This is a dedicated gluten-free and plant-based kitchen: the restaurant states all menu items are gluten-free and plant-based, the kitchen contains no gluten or animal products, and customers are asked not to bring those items into the dining area. Because there is no wheat in the kitchen at all, the usual ramen cross-contamination risks (shared noodle water, shared broth) are largely removed.
A celiac-conscious diner highlighted the advantage of an all-gluten-free operation, noting 'not having to worry about cross contamination when it comes to soup especially.'
The noodles themselves are gluten-free, made from rice flour kneaded with kelp rather than wheat; reviewers describe them as smooth and slightly spaghetti-like.
Unlike most Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, this restaurant specifically uses gluten-free soy sauce in its broth and seasoning, so the soup is described as gluten-free.
The entire operation is vegan with no animal products in the kitchen, which removes the typical risk of vegan cross-contact from shared meat or dashi-based broths found in conventional ramen shops.
Tabelog reviews describe it as a completely vegan ramen shop where all menu items are plant-based.
Reviewers praise the allergen transparency, noting items are 'very clearly labeled for all kinds of allergens, such as soy, gluten and wheat.'

The restaurant says it can accommodate other specific allergies on request and offers nut-free and mushroom-free options. Given the soy milk broth, soy-allergic diners should confirm options directly, as the menu is soy-forward.

A genuinely dedicated gluten-free and vegan kitchen founded specifically to serve people with allergies and dietary restrictions, which is rare for ramen and unusually safe for celiac diners compared to typical wheat-and-dashi ramen shops.
Gluten-free soy sauce and rice-flour noodles mean the broth and noodles are both made without wheat.
Reviewers report clear allergen labeling and a celiac diner specifically noted not having to worry about cross-contamination in the soup.

The kitchen operates with no wheat in the building at all -- the cafe states that every menu item is gluten-free and contains no wheat, which structurally reduces the risk of wheat cross-contact compared with a mixed kitchen. No specific protocol (separate prep surfaces, shared equipment) is documented, so celiac diners should still confirm details directly.

No specific information was found on whether soy sauce or seasonings used are wheat-free. Because most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, anyone with celiac disease should confirm the brand or alternative used before ordering.

The entire menu is vegan -- no dairy, eggs, or other animal products are used anywhere on the menu -- so the risk of animal-product cross-contact is inherently low. Vegan cheese is made from fermented cashew nuts, which is relevant for those with tree-nut allergies.
100% vegan and 100% gluten-free kitchen: every menu item is plant-based and made without dairy, eggs, or wheat, using organic and additive-free ingredients.
Signature gluten-free pizza uses a rice-flour crust and cashew-based vegan cheese rather than wheat dough.

The entire shop is dedicated gluten-free: every item on the menu is gluten-free, with crepes built on a fermented rice-flour batter rather than wheat. Because there is no wheat flour used anywhere, the risk of gluten cross-contact is inherently low.
A celiac travel writer describes it as 'an excellent 100% gluten free crepe restaurant' and ate two crepes there without noting any issue, treating it as a safe dedicated venue.

This is a creperie, not a soy-sauce-heavy kitchen, and the shop actually sells bottles of gluten-free soy sauce, indicating awareness of the wheat-in-soy-sauce issue. Savory crepes are gluten-free across the board, but it is still worth confirming with staff that any savory sauce on your specific crepe is the gluten-free version.

The whole menu is plant-based, so there is no animal dairy or egg used in the standard dough; the crepe batter itself is naturally vegan and dairy-free cream, cheese and chocolate alternatives are used throughout.
Reviewers across platforms consistently describe the staff as kind, helpful and attentive to allergies and dietary needs.
A fully dedicated gluten-free and vegan kitchen using a fermented organic rice-flour batter, which removes wheat from the premises entirely.
Celiac travelers single it out as one of the safer, dedicated gluten-free stops in Kyoto.
Vegan diners praise the abundant plant-based options, including the homemade soy-milk whipped cream and vegan cheese.

name: Hirose Okomeya Cafe (廣瀬米穀店 お米屋カフェ)

claims.text: 全商品を米粉100％で製造し、小麦粉・白砂糖は一切使用していない（Made with 100% rice flour; no wheat flour or white sugar used at all).

It is a rice merchant / rice mill and food shop (自家精米), not a certified dedicated gluten-free kitchen — the product line is entirely rice-based and the shop sells no wheat products, but celiacs should confirm on the day that no wheat is handled or stored on-site.
お米パン／こめやパンは米・米油・メープル・塩・米種・酵母・お湯のみで焼く植物性の食品（rice bread is plant-based). シフォンケーキには卵が含まれる（chiffon contains egg).
店主は米粉マイスター・五ツ星お米マイスターの有資格者で、グルテンフリーを明確に掲げている（Owner is a certified rice-flour master and explicitly markets the shop as gluten-free).
米屋なので小麦製品を扱わず、カフェのお菓子・パンはすべて米粉100％（A rice shop that handles no wheat products; all café sweets and bread are 100% rice flour).
自家精米したての新鮮な米から作るグルテンフリーのお米パンとシフォンケーキ（Gluten-free rice bread and chiffon made from freshly in-house-milled rice).

name: Ikariya Beika Kyoto (イカリヤベイカ京都)

claims.text: 焼き菓子の製造ラインは自家製粉の米粉のみで小麦粉を使用しない専門工房のため、製品自体の小麦クロスコンタミ・リスクは低い。
個人ブログでは『メニューはすべて米粉を使ったグルテンフリー』と報告されているが、店奥のイートインで供する飲み物・付け合わせに小麦品がないかは公式には未確認。
バウムクーヘンは卵・乳(バター)を含むため、ヴィーガン品との交差接触管理に関する情報はなく、そもそもヴィーガン提供品が確認できない。
米菓職人が自家製粉した米粉で丁寧に焼き上げると明記されるが、個別の小麦アレルギー対応プロトコルの記載は見当たらない。
専門店として全焼き菓子が米粉ベースの小麦不使用で、グルテンフリーの土産・スイーツとして京都のGFガイドでも紹介されている。
生米を工房内で自家製粉するなど原材料管理にこだわり、JR京都伊勢丹でもグルテンフリーバウムとして販売実績がある。
